title: Are You Sabotaging Your Own Classroom Management Success? ement-success/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to a recurring reader question about disadvantaged students, Linsin argues that a negative attitude, not circumstance, is the real barrier to effective classroom management. He presents seven principles that form the mindset needed for exceptional classroom management: believing you can succeed, believing in your students, refusing to make excuses, taking full responsibility for the classroom, committing to doing what's right even when it's hard, ignoring pessimistic colleagues, and continually studying classroom management as a craft. He insists that teachers in the most difficult circumstances imaginable have achieved dream classes, and that the same is possible for any reader willing to change their thinking and commit to the process.
points: A negative, defeatist attitude — not a student's background or circumstances — is the real obstacle standing between a teacher and a well-managed classroom.
Teachers must believe, as a foregone conclusion rather than a mere possibility, that they can create the class they want.
Making excuses based on students' home lives or neighborhoods amounts to giving up on both the students and oneself.
Teachers must take ownership of everything happening in their classroom regardless of whether they are directly responsible for a given incident.
Becoming a genuine 'student of classroom management' — studying and understanding strategies deeply rather than half-learning them — is essential to success.
quotes: The fact is, it doesn’t matter where you teach or who shows up on your roster, the well-behaved classroom you long for is within your grasp.
A defeatist point of view will undermine everything you do—sealing your fate to a career of frustration, disappointment, and dissatisfaction.
In order to create the class you really want, you have to believe deep down that you can—not merely as a possibility, but as a foregone conclusion that you will.
The truth is, offering excuses, even in the privacy of your own mind, is akin to giving up on your students—as well as on yourself.
By taking responsibility for everything within the four walls of your classroom, you instantly become a better, more effective teacher.
There are scores of teachers all over the world, some in the most difficult circumstances imaginable, who this very minute are enjoying the dream class they’ve always wanted.
